Optimal functions with spectral constraints in hypercubes

Journal: Arxiv
Alexandr Valyuzhenich Email: graphkiper@mail.ru Address: Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology, Dolgoprudny, Russia
Abstract

The nn-dimensional hypercube has n+1n+1 distinct eigenvalues n−2​in-2i, 0≤i≤n0\leq i\leq n, with corresponding eigenspaces Ui​(n)U_{i}(n). In 2021 it was proved by the author that if a function with non-empty support belongs to the direct sum Ui​(n)⊕Ui+1​(n)⊕…⊕Uj​(n)U_{i}(n)\oplus U_{i+1}(n)\oplus\ldots\oplus U_{j}(n), where 0≤i≤j≤n0\leq i\leq j\leq n, then it has at least max⁡(2i,2n−j)\max(2^{i},2^{n-j}) non-zeros. In this work we give a characterization of functions achieving this bound.

Keywords:
hypercube, eigenfunction, eigenfunctions of graphs, minimum support, trade, [t][t]-trade
2010 MSC
05C50, 05B30

1 Introduction

There are the following extremal problems for eigenfunctions of graphs.

Problem 1.

Let GG be a graph and let λ\lambda be an eigenvalue of GG. Find the minimum cardinality of the support of a λ\lambda-eigenfunction of GG.

Problem 2.

Let GG be a graph and let λ\lambda be an eigenvalue of GG. Characterize λ\lambda-eigenfunctions of GG with the minimum cardinality of the support.

During the last years, Problems 1 and 2 have been actively studied for various families of distance-regular graphs [1, 5, 6, 8, 11, 13, 14, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20] and Cayley graphs on the symmetric group [7]. In particular, Problem 1 is completely solved for all eigenvalues of the Hamming graph [8, 17, 18] and asymptotically solved for all eigenvalues of the Johnson graph [20]. In more details, Problems 1 and 2 are discussed in a recent survey [15].

The Hamming graph H⁡(n,q)H(n,q) is defined as follows. The vertex set of H⁡(n,q)H(n,q) is ℤqn\mathbb{Z}_{q}^{n}, and two vertices are adjacent if they differ in exactly one coordinate. The adjacency matrix of H⁡(n,q)H(n,q) has n+1n+1 distinct eigenvalues n⁡(q−1)−q⋅in(q-1)-q\cdot i, where 0≤i≤n0\leq i\leq n. Let U[i,j]​(n,q)U_{[i,j]}(n,q), where 0≤i≤j≤n0\leq i\leq j\leq n, denote the direct sum of eigenspaces of H⁡(n,q)H(n,q) corresponding to consecutive eigenvalues from n⁡(q−1)−q⋅in(q-1)-q\cdot i to n⁡(q−1)−q⋅jn(q-1)-q\cdot j. The support of a real-valued function ff is denoted by S⁡(f)S(f).

Let 0≤i≤j≤n0\leq i\leq j\leq n. Denote

mi,j​(n,q)=minf∈U[i,j]​(n,q),f≢0⁡|S⁡(f)|.m_{i,j}(n,q)=\min_{f\in U_{[i,j](n,q)},f\not\equiv 0}|S(f)|.

A function f∈U[i,j]​(n,q)f\in U_{[i,j]}(n,q) is called optimal in the space U[i,j]​(n,q)U_{[i,j]}(n,q) if |S⁡(f)|=mi,j​(n,q)|S(f)|=m_{i,j}(n,q). In this work we consider the following natural generalizations of Problems 1 and 2 for the Hamming graph.

Problem 3.

Let n≥1n\geq 1, q≥2q\geq 2 and 0≤i≤j≤n0\leq i\leq j\leq n. Find mi,j​(n,q)m_{i,j}(n,q).

Problem 4.

Let n≥1n\geq 1, q≥2q\geq 2 and 0≤i≤j≤n0\leq i\leq j\leq n. Characterize functions that are optimal in the space U[i,j]​(n,q)U_{[i,j]}(n,q).

Problem 3 is completely solved for all n≥1n\geq 1 and q≥2q\geq 2 in [17, 18]. Moreover, Problem 4 is solved for q≥3q\geq 3, i+j≤ni+j\leq n and q≥5q\geq 5, i=ji=j, i>n2i>\frac{n}{2} in [17]. In this work we solve Problem 4 for q=2q=2 and arbitrary nn. The main ideas of the proof are the following. For i+j≥ni+j\geq n, we prove that functions that are optimal in the space U[i,j]​(n,2)U_{[i,j]}(n,2) correspond to some [i−1][i-1]-trades in H⁡(n,2)H(n,2) (for more information on [t][t]-trades see [4, 10]). Then we apply a characterization of [t][t]-trades of size 2t+12^{t+1} obtained by D. Krotov in [10]. Finally, using the bipartiteness of H⁡(n,2)H(n,2), we reduce the case i+j≤ni+j\leq n to the case i+j≥ni+j\geq n.

The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we introduce basic definitions. In Section 3, we give preliminary results. In Section 4, we present constructions of functions that are optimal in the space U[i,j]​(n,2)U_{[i,j]}(n,2). In Section 5, we characterize functions that are optimal in the space U[i,j]​(n,2)U_{[i,j]}(n,2). In Section 6, we discuss the properties of the spectrum of optimal functions.

2 Basic definitions

The eigenvalues of a graph are the eigenvalues of its adjacency matrix. Let GG be a graph with vertex set VV and let λ\lambda be an eigenvalue of GG. The set of neighbors of a vertex xx is denoted by N⁡(x)N(x). A function f:V⟶ℝf:V\longrightarrow{\mathbb{R}} is called a λ\lambda-eigenfunction of GG if f≢0f\not\equiv 0 and the equality

λ⋅f⁡(x)=∑y∈N⁡(x)f⁡(y)\lambda\cdot f(x)=\sum_{y\in{N(x)}}f(y) (1)

holds for any vertex x∈Vx\in V. The set of functions f:V⟶ℝf:V\longrightarrow{\mathbb{R}} satisfying (1) for any vertex x∈Vx\in V is called a λ\lambda-eigenspace of GG. The support of a function f:V⟶ℝf:V\longrightarrow{\mathbb{R}} is the set S⁡(f)={x∈V|f⁡(x)≠0}S(f)=\{x\in V\penalty\ |\penalty\ f(x)\neq 0\}. Denote |f|=|S⁡(f)||f|=|S(f)|.

Given a graph GG, denote by U⁡(G)U(G) the set of all real-valued functions defined on the vertex set of GG. Note that the set U⁡(G)U(G) forms a vector space over ℝ\mathbb{R}.

The nn-dimensional hypercube H⁡(n)H(n) is defined as follows. The vertex set of H⁡(n)H(n) is ℤ2n\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{n}, and two vertices are adjacent if they differ in exactly one coordinate. This graph has n+1n+1 distinct eigenvalues λi​(n)=n−2​i\lambda_{i}(n)=n-2i, where 0≤i≤n0\leq i\leq n. Denote by Ui​(n)U_{i}(n) the λi​(n)\lambda_{i}(n)-eigenspace of H⁡(n)H(n). The direct sum of subspaces

Ui​(n)⊕Ui+1​(n)⊕…⊕Uj​(n)U_{i}(n)\oplus U_{i+1}(n)\oplus\ldots\oplus U_{j}(n)

for 0≤i≤j≤n0\leq i\leq j\leq n is denoted by U[i,j]​(n)U_{[i,j]}(n). Denote U⁡(n)=U⁡(H⁡(n))U(n)=U(H(n)).

Let G1=(V1,E1)G_{1}=(V_{1},E_{1}) and G2=(V2,E2)G_{2}=(V_{2},E_{2}) be two graphs. The Cartesian product G1​□​G2G_{1}\square G_{2} of graphs G1G_{1} and G2G_{2} is defined as follows. The vertex set of G1​□​G2G_{1}\square G_{2} is V1×V2V_{1}\times V_{2}; and any two vertices (x1,y1)(x_{1},y_{1}) and (x2,y2)(x_{2},y_{2}) are adjacent if and only if either x1=x2x_{1}=x_{2} and y1y_{1} is adjacent to y2y_{2} in G2G_{2}, or y1=y2y_{1}=y_{2} and x1x_{1} is adjacent to x2x_{2} in G1G_{1}.

Suppose G1=(V1,E1)G_{1}=(V_{1},E_{1}) and G2=(V2,E2)G_{2}=(V_{2},E_{2}) are two graphs. Let f1:V1⟶ℝf_{1}:V_{1}\longrightarrow{\mathbb{R}} and f2:V2⟶ℝf_{2}:V_{2}\longrightarrow{\mathbb{R}}. Denote G=G1​□​G2G=G_{1}\square G_{2}. We define the tensor product f1⊗f2f_{1}\otimes f_{2} on the vertices of GG by the following rule:

(f1⊗f2)​(x,y)=f1​(x)​f2​(y)(f_{1}\otimes f_{2})(x,y)=f_{1}(x)f_{2}(y)

for (x,y)∈V⁡(G)=V1×V2(x,y)\in V(G)=V_{1}\times V_{2}.

Let ff be a real-valued function defined on the vertices of H⁡(n)H(n) and let k∈{0,1}k\in\{0,1\}, r∈{1,…,n}r\in\{1,\ldots,n\}. We define a function fkrf_{k}^{r} on the vertices of H⁡(n−1)H(n-1) as follows: for any vertex y=(y1,…,yr−1,yr+1,…,yn)y=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{r-1},y_{r+1},\ldots,y_{n}) of H⁡(n−1)H(n-1)

fkr​(y)=f⁡(y1,…,yr−1,k,yr+1,…,yn).f_{k}^{r}(y)=f(y_{1},\ldots,y_{r-1},k,y_{r+1},\ldots,y_{n}).

For a vector u∈ℤ2nu\in\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{n}, where u=(u1,…,un)u=(u_{1},\ldots,u_{n}), we define a function χu\chi_{u} on the vertices of H⁡(n)H(n) as follows:

χu​(x1,…,xn)=(−1)u1​x1+…+un​xn.\chi_{u}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=(-1)^{u_{1}x_{1}+\ldots+u_{n}x_{n}}.

The functions χu\chi_{u}, where u∈ℤ2nu\in\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{n}, are also known as the characters of the group ℤ2n\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{n}.

The weight of a vector x∈ℤ2nx\in\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{n}, denoted by wt⁡(x)\mathrm{wt}(x), is the number of its non-zero coordinates.

Let AA and BB be two finite subsets of ℤ\mathbb{Z}. Denote

A+B={c∈ℤ|c=a+b,a∈A,b∈B}.A+B=\{c\in\mathbb{Z}\penalty\ |\penalty\ c=a+b,a\in A,b\in B\}.

Let {i1,…,im}\{i_{1},\ldots,i_{m}\} be an mm-element subset of {1,2,…,n}\{1,2,\ldots,n\} and let ai∈{0,1}a_{i}\in\{0,1\} for all 1≤i≤m1\leq i\leq m. Denote

Γi1,…,ima1,…,am={(x1,…,xn)∈ℤ2n|xi1=a1,…,xim=am}.\Gamma_{i_{1},\ldots,i_{m}}^{a_{1},\ldots,a_{m}}=\{(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{n}\penalty\ |\penalty\ x_{i_{1}}=a_{1},\ldots,x_{i_{m}}=a_{m}\}.

For m∈{0,1,…,n}m\in\{0,1,\ldots,n\}, a set Γ⊆ℤ2n\Gamma\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{n} is called an (n−m)(n-m)-face if there exist an mm-element subset {i1,…,im}\{i_{1},\ldots,i_{m}\} of {1,2,…,n}\{1,2,\ldots,n\} and numbers a1,…,am∈{0,1}a_{1},\ldots,a_{m}\in\{0,1\} such that Γ=Γi1,…,ima1,…,am\Gamma=\Gamma_{i_{1},\ldots,i_{m}}^{a_{1},\ldots,a_{m}}.

Recall that the set U⁡(n)U(n) forms a vector space over ℝ\mathbb{R}. We define an inner product on this vector space as follows:

⟨f,g⟩=12n​∑x∈ℤ2nf⁡(x)​g​(x)\langle f,g\rangle=\frac{1}{2^{n}}\sum_{x\in\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{n}}f(x)g(x)

Two functions f∈U⁡(n)f\in U(n) and g∈U⁡(n)g\in U(n) are called orthogonal if ⟨f,g⟩=0\langle f,g\rangle=0.

A pair {T0,T1}\{T_{0},T_{1}\} of two disjoint nonempty subsets of ℤ2n\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{n} is called a [t][t]-trade in H⁡(n)H(n) if every (n−t)(n-t)-face contains the same number of elements from T0T_{0} and from T1T_{1}. For a subset AA of ℤ2n\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{n}, let 𝟏A\mathbf{1}_{A} denote the characteristic function of AA in ℤ2n\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{n}.

For every non-negative integer rr and every positive integer n≥rn\geq r, the Reed–Muller code ℛ​ℳ​(r,n)\mathcal{RM}(r,n) of order rr is the set of all nn-variable Boolean functions of algebraic degree at most rr.

Let GG be a bipartite graph with parts V1V_{1} and V2V_{2}. Suppose that ff is a real-valued function defined on the vertices of GG. We define a function f′f^{\prime} on the vertices of GG by the following rule:

f′​(x)={f⁡(x),if x∈V1;−f⁡(x),if x∈V2.f^{\prime}(x)=\begin{cases}f(x),&\text{if $x\in V_{1}$;}\\ -f(x),&\text{if $x\in V_{2}$.}\end{cases}

For a function f∈U⁡(n)f\in U(n), we define a function f~\widetilde{f} on the vertices of H⁡(n)H(n) as follows:

f~​(x1,…,xn)=(−1)x1+…+xn⋅f⁡(x1,…,xn).\widetilde{f}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=(-1)^{x_{1}+\ldots+x_{n}}\cdot f(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}).

Any function f∈U⁡(n)f\in U(n) can be uniquely represented in the following form:

f=∑i=0nfi,f=\sum_{i=0}^{n}f_{i},

where fi∈Ui​(n)f_{i}\in U_{i}(n) for any 0≤i≤n0\leq i\leq n. The spectrum of a function f∈U⁡(n)f\in U(n) is the set

Spec⁡(f)={0≤i≤n|fi≢0}.\mathrm{Spec}(f)=\{0\leq i\leq n\penalty\ |\penalty\ f_{i}\not\equiv 0\}.

Two functions f∈U⁡(n)f\in U(n) and g∈U⁡(n)g\in U(n) are called equivalent if there exist an automorphism π\pi of H⁡(n)H(n) and a real non-zero constant cc such that the equality g⁡(x)=c⋅f⁡(π⁡(x))g(x)=c\cdot f(\pi(x)) holds for any vertex xx of H⁡(n)H(n). We denote this equivalence by f∼gf\sim g.

3 Preliminaries

In this section, we give preliminary results. The following lemma is a special case of Corollary 1 proved in [17].

Lemma 1.

Let f1∈Ui​(m)f_{1}\in U_{i}(m) and f2∈Uj​(n)f_{2}\in U_{j}(n). Then f1⊗f2∈Ui+j​(m+n)f_{1}\otimes f_{2}\in U_{i+j}(m+n).

The following result is a special case of Lemma 4 proved in [17].

Lemma 2.

Let f∈U[i,j]​(n)f\in{U_{[i,j]}(n)} and r∈{1,2,…,n}r\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}. Then the following statements are true:

  1. 1.

    f0r−f1r∈U[i−1,j−1]​(n−1)f_{0}^{r}-f_{1}^{r}\in{U_{[i-1,j-1]}(n-1)}.

  2. 2.

    f0r+f1r∈U[i,j]​(n−1)f_{0}^{r}+f_{1}^{r}\in{U_{[i,j]}(n-1)}.

  3. 3.

    fkr∈U[i−1,j]​(n−1)f_{k}^{r}\in{U_{[i-1,j]}(n-1)} for k∈{0,1}k\in\{0,1\}.

Lemma 3.

Let f∈U[i,j]​(n)f\in{U_{[i,j]}(n)} and r∈{1,2,…,n}r\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}. Then there are functions gg and hh such that f0r=g+hf_{0}^{r}=g+h, f1r=g−hf_{1}^{r}=g-h and g∈U[i,j]​(n−1)g\in U_{[i,j]}(n-1), h∈U[i−1,j−1]​(n−1)h\in U_{[i-1,j-1]}(n-1).

Proof.

Denote g=12​(f0r+f1r)g=\frac{1}{2}(f_{0}^{r}+f_{1}^{r}) and h=12​(f0r−f1r)h=\frac{1}{2}(f_{0}^{r}-f_{1}^{r}). Then we have f0r=g+hf_{0}^{r}=g+h and f1r=g−hf_{1}^{r}=g-h. In addition, by Lemma 2 we obtain that g∈U[i,j]​(n−1)g\in U_{[i,j]}(n-1) and h∈U[i−1,j−1]​(n−1)h\in U_{[i-1,j-1]}(n-1). ∎

We will use Lemma 3 in the proof of Lemma 17. The following two properties of the characters of ℤ2n\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{n} are well-known.

Lemma 4.

The following statements hold:

  1. 1.

    The set {χu|u∈ℤ2n}\{\chi_{u}\penalty\ |\penalty\ u\in\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{n}\} forms an orthonormal basis of the vector space U⁡(n)U(n).

  2. 2.

    For every 0≤i≤n0\leq i\leq n, the set {χu|u∈ℤ2n,wt(u)=i}\{\chi_{u}\penalty\ |\penalty\ u\in\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{n},\mathrm{wt}(u)=i\} forms a basis of the vector space Ui​(n)U_{i}(n).

We will use Lemma 4 for the proofs of Lemmas 6, 7, 8 and 15. The following result about the Cartesian product of graphs is well-known.

Lemma 5.

Let G1G_{1} and G2G_{2} be graphs with mm and nn vertices. If f1,…,fmf_{1},\ldots,f_{m} and g1,…,gng_{1},\ldots,g_{n} are orthogonal bases for the vector spaces U⁡(G1)U(G_{1}) and U⁡(G2)U(G_{2}), then the set

{fi⊗gj|i∈{1,…,m},j∈{1,…,n}}\{f_{i}\otimes g_{j}\penalty\ |\penalty\ i\in\{1,\ldots,m\},j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\}

forms an orthogonal basis of the vector space U⁡(G1​□​G2)U(G_{1}\square G_{2}).

Using Lemmas 4 and 5, we immediately obtain the following result.

Lemma 6.

The set {χu⊗χv|u∈ℤ2m,v∈ℤ2n}\{\chi_{u}\otimes\chi_{v}\penalty\ |\penalty\ u\in\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{m},v\in\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{n}\} forms an orthogonal basis of the vector space U⁡(m+n)U(m+n).

Lemma 7.

Let f1∈U⁡(m)f_{1}\in U(m) and f2∈U⁡(n)f_{2}\in U(n). Then

Spec⁡(f1⊗f2)=Spec⁡(f1)+Spec⁡(f2).\mathrm{Spec}(f_{1}\otimes f_{2})=\mathrm{Spec}(f_{1})+\mathrm{Spec}(f_{2}).
Proof.

It follows from Lemmas 4, 6 and 1. ∎

We will use Lemma 7 in the proof of Lemma 16. The following theorem is a combination of the results proved in [18] (see [18, Theorems 3 and 4]).

Theorem 1.

Let f∈U[i,j]​(n)f\in U_{[i,j]}(n) and f≢0f\not\equiv 0. Then the following statements hold:

  1. 1.

    If i+j≥ni+j\geq n, then |f|≥2i|f|\geq 2^{i} and this bound is sharp.

  2. 2.

    If i+j≤ni+j\leq n, then |f|≥2n−j|f|\geq 2^{n-j} and this bound is sharp.

We will use Theorem 1 in the proof of Lemma 17.

Lemma 8.

Let f∈Ui​(n)f\in U_{i}(n), where 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n. Then for every (n−i+1)(n-i+1)-face Γ\Gamma it holds ∑x∈Γf⁡(x)=0\sum_{x\in\Gamma}f(x)=0.

Proof.

Suppose that Γ\Gamma is an (n−i+1)(n-i+1)-face. It is easy to check that the function 𝟏Γ\mathbf{1}_{\Gamma} is orthogonal to χu\chi_{u} for any u∈ℤ2nu\in\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{n} of weight ii. Then by Lemma 4 we obtain that 𝟏Γ\mathbf{1}_{\Gamma} is orthogonal to an arbitrary function from the space Ui​(n)U_{i}(n). So, the functions 𝟏Γ\mathbf{1}_{\Gamma} and ff are orthogonal and we have ∑x∈Γf⁡(x)=0\sum_{x\in\Gamma}f(x)=0. ∎

The following result was obtained in [10] (see the last paragraph in the proof of Theorem 1).

Lemma 9.

Let {T0,T1}\{T_{0},T_{1}\} be a [t][t]-trade in H⁡(n)H(n). Then 𝟏T0∪T1∈ℛ​ℳ​(n−t−1,n)\mathbf{1}_{T_{0}\cup T_{1}}\in\mathcal{RM}(n-t-1,n).

The following fact is well known in coding theory (for example, see [12, Chapter 13, Theorem 5] or [3, Chapter 4, Theorem 8]).

Lemma 10.

Any Boolean function from ℛ​ℳ​(r,n)\mathcal{RM}(r,n) of weight 2n−r2^{n-r} is the characteristic function of an (n−r)(n-r)-dimensional affine subspace of ℤ2n\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{n}.

The following lemma was proved in [10].

Lemma 11 ([10], Proposition 1).

An affine subspace T⊂ℤ2nT\subset\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{n} of dimension t+1t+1 can be split into a [t][t]-trade {T0,T1}\{T_{0},T_{1}\} if and only if it is a translation of the linear span of mutually disjoint base subsets.

We will use Lemmas 8, 9, 10 and 11 in the proof of Theorem 2. The following fact is well known in spectral graph theory (for example, see [2, Section 1.3.6]).

Lemma 12.

Let GG be a bipartite graph. If ff is a λ\lambda-eigenfunction of GG, then f′f^{\prime} is a (-λ\lambda)-eigenfunction of GG.

Since H⁡(n)H(n) is bipartite and λi​(n)=−λn−i​(n)\lambda_{i}(n)=-\lambda_{n-i}(n), by Lemma 12 we immediately obtain the following result.

Lemma 13.

If f∈Ui​(n)f\in U_{i}(n), then f~∈Un−i​(n)\widetilde{f}\in U_{n-i}(n).

Using the previous lemma for Uk​(n)U_{k}(n), where i≤k≤ji\leq k\leq j, we obtain the following result.

Lemma 14.

If f∈U[i,j]​(n)f\in U_{[i,j]}(n), then f~∈U[n−j,n−i]​(n)\widetilde{f}\in U_{[n-j,n-i]}(n).

We will use Lemma 14 in the proof of Theorem 2.

4 Constructions of functions with the minimum cardinality of the support

In this section, we give constructions of functions that are optimal in the space U[i,j]​(n)U_{[i,j]}(n). We also find the spectrum of these functions.

For k≥1k\geq 1, we define a function φk\varphi_{k} on the vertices of H⁡(k)H(k) by the following rule:

φk​(x)={1,if x is the all-zeros vector;−1,if x is the all-ones vector;0,otherwise.\varphi_{k}(x)=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if $x$ is the all-zeros vector;}\\ -1,&\text{if $x$ is the all-ones vector;}\\ 0,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

For k≥1k\geq 1, we define a function ψk\psi_{k} on the vertices of H⁡(k)H(k) by the following rule:

ψk​(x)={1,if x is the all-zeros vector;1,if x is the all-ones vector;0,otherwise.\psi_{k}(x)=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if $x$ is the all-zeros vector;}\\ 1,&\text{if $x$ is the all-ones vector;}\\ 0,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

For k≥1k\geq 1, we define a function IkI_{k} on the vertices of H⁡(k)H(k) by the following rule:

Ik​(x)={1,if x is the all-zeros vector;0,otherwise.I_{k}(x)=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if $x$ is the all-zeros vector;}\\ 0,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

Lemma 15.

The following statements are true:

  1. 1.

    Spec⁡(φ2​k+1)={1,3,…,2​k+1}\mathrm{Spec}(\varphi_{2k+1})=\{1,3,\ldots,2k+1\} for k≥1k\geq 1 and Spec⁡(φ1)={1}\mathrm{Spec}(\varphi_{1})=\{1\}.

  2. 2.

    Spec⁡(φ2​k)={1,3,…,2​k−1}\mathrm{Spec}(\varphi_{2k})=\{1,3,\ldots,2k-1\} for k≥2k\geq 2 and Spec⁡(φ2)={1}\mathrm{Spec}(\varphi_{2})=\{1\}.

  3. 3.

    Spec⁡(ψ2​k+1)={0,2,…,2​k}\mathrm{Spec}(\psi_{2k+1})=\{0,2,\ldots,2k\} for k≥1k\geq 1 and Spec⁡(ψ1)={0}\mathrm{Spec}(\psi_{1})=\{0\}.

  4. 4.

    Spec⁡(Ik)={0,1,…,k}\mathrm{Spec}(I_{k})=\{0,1,\ldots,k\} for k≥1k\geq 1.

Proof.

Let us consider the function φn\varphi_{n}. By Lemma 4, there exist the real numbers cuc_{u}, where u∈ℤ2nu\in\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{n}, such that

φn=∑u∈ℤ2ncu​χu.\varphi_{n}=\sum_{u\in\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{n}}c_{u}\chi_{u}.

Then we have

⟨φn,χu⟩=⟨∑u∈ℤ2ncu​χu,χu⟩=cu​⟨χu,χu⟩=cu.\langle\varphi_{n},\chi_{u}\rangle=\langle\sum_{u\in\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{n}}c_{u}\chi_{u},\chi_{u}\rangle=c_{u}\langle\chi_{u},\chi_{u}\rangle=c_{u}.

On the other hand,

⟨φn,χu⟩=12n​∑x∈ℤ2nφn​(x)​χu​(x)=12n​(1−(−1)u1+…+un).\langle\varphi_{n},\chi_{u}\rangle=\frac{1}{2^{n}}\sum_{x\in\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{n}}\varphi_{n}(x)\chi_{u}(x)=\frac{1}{2^{n}}(1-(-1)^{u_{1}+\ldots+u_{n}}).

Hence

cu=12n​(1−(−1)u1+…+un)c_{u}=\frac{1}{2^{n}}(1-(-1)^{u_{1}+\ldots+u_{n}})

for any u∈ℤ2nu\in\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{n}. So, we have

cu={12n−1,if wt⁡(u) is odd;0,if wt⁡(u) is even.c_{u}=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{2^{n-1}},&\text{if $\mathrm{wt}(u)$ is odd;}\\ 0,&\text{if $\mathrm{wt}(u)$ is even.}\end{cases}

Using Lemma 4, we obtain that Spec⁡(φn)\mathrm{Spec}(\varphi_{n}) consists of odd numbers belonging to the set {1,…,n}\{1,\ldots,n\}.

The proofs for the functions ψn\psi_{n} and InI_{n} are similar. ∎

Lemma 16.

Let nn be a positive integer and n=n1+…+nk+m1+…+mℓ+rn=n_{1}+\ldots+n_{k}+m_{1}+\ldots+m_{\ell}+r, where n1,…,nkn_{1},\ldots,n_{k} are odd positive integers, m1,…,mℓm_{1},\ldots,m_{\ell} are even positive integers, kk, ℓ\ell and rr are nonnegative integers. Then the following statements hold:

    Spec⁡(f)={k+ℓ,k+ℓ+2,…,n−ℓ}\mathrm{Spec}(f)=\{k+\ell,k+\ell+2,\ldots,n-\ell\}

    for r=0r=0.

    Let f=ψn1⊗⋯⊗ψnk⊗φm1⊗⋯⊗φmℓ⊗Irf=\psi_{n_{1}}\otimes\cdots\otimes\psi_{n_{k}}\otimes\varphi_{m_{1}}\otimes\cdots\otimes\varphi_{m_{\ell}}\otimes I_{r}. Then f∈U[ℓ,n−k−ℓ]​(n)f\in U_{[\ell,n-k-\ell]}(n) and |f|=2k+ℓ|f|=2^{k+\ell}. Moreover,

    Spec⁡(f)={ℓ,ℓ+1,…,n−k−ℓ}\mathrm{Spec}(f)=\{\ell,\ell+1,\ldots,n-k-\ell\}

    Spec⁡(f)={ℓ,ℓ+2,…,n−k−ℓ}\mathrm{Spec}(f)=\{\ell,\ell+2,\ldots,n-k-\ell\}

    for r=0r=0.

Proof.

Let us consider the first case. By Lemma 7 we have

Spec⁡(f)=Spec⁡(φn1)+…+Spec⁡(φnk)+…+Spec⁡(φm1)+…+Spec⁡(φmℓ)+Spec⁡(Ir).\mathrm{Spec}(f)=\mathrm{Spec}(\varphi_{n_{1}})+\ldots+\mathrm{Spec}(\varphi_{n_{k}})+\ldots+\mathrm{Spec}(\varphi_{m_{1}})+\ldots+\mathrm{Spec}(\varphi_{m_{\ell}})+\mathrm{Spec}(I_{r}).

Then applying Lemma 15, we obtain that

Spec⁡(f)={k+ℓ,k+ℓ+1,…,n−ℓ}\mathrm{Spec}(f)=\{k+\ell,k+\ell+1,\ldots,n-\ell\}

for r>0r>0 and

for r=0r=0. Using the equality |f1⊗f2|=|f1|⋅|f2||f_{1}\otimes f_{2}|=|f_{1}|\cdot|f_{2}|, we see that |f|=2k+ℓ|f|=2^{k+\ell}.

The proof for the second case is similar. ∎

5 Main results

In this section, we prove the main theorem of this paper. Firstly, we prove the following result.

Lemma 17.

Let f∈U[i,j]​(n)f\in U_{[i,j]}(n), where i+j≥ni+j\geq n. If |f|=2i|f|=2^{i}, then ff takes values from the set {−a,0,a}\{-a,0,a\}, where aa is a positive real number.

Proof.

Let us prove this lemma by induction on nn, ii and jj. If i=0i=0, then |f|=1|f|=1 and the claim of the lemma holds. So, we can assume that i≥1i\geq 1. If n=1n=1, then i=j=1i=j=1. Then f∈U1​(1)f\in U_{1}(1) and the claim of the lemma holds.

Let us prove the induction step for n≥2n\geq 2 and i≥1i\geq 1. Let us consider the functions f0nf_{0}^{n} and f1nf_{1}^{n}. Denote fk=fknf_{k}=f_{k}^{n} for k∈{0,1}k\in\{0,1\}. Lemma 3 implies that there are functions gg and hh such that f0=g+hf_{0}=g+h, f1=g−hf_{1}=g-h and g∈U[i,j]​(n−1)g\in U_{[i,j]}(n-1), h∈U[i−1,j−1]​(n−1)h\in U_{[i-1,j-1]}(n-1). Let us consider two cases.

In the first case we suppose that g≡0g\equiv 0. In this case we have |h|=12​|f|=2i−1|h|=\frac{1}{2}|f|=2^{i-1}. Let us show that i+j≥n+1i+j\geq n+1. Indeed, if i+j=ni+j=n, then |h|≥2i|h|\geq 2^{i} due to Theorem 1. Since |h|=2i−1|h|=2^{i-1}, we get a contradiction. So, in this case we have i+j≥n+1i+j\geq n+1. Applying the induction assumption for hh, we obtain that hh takes values from the set {−a,0,a}\{-a,0,a\}, where aa is a positive real number. Therefore, ff also takes values from the set {−a,0,a}\{-a,0,a\}.

In the second case we suppose that g≢0g\not\equiv 0. Since g∈U[i,j]​(n−1)g\in U_{[i,j]}(n-1), by Theorem 1 we obtain that |g|≥2i|g|\geq 2^{i}. Then we have

|f|=|f0|+|f1|≥|f0+f1|=|g|≥2i.|f|=|f_{0}|+|f_{1}|\geq|f_{0}+f_{1}|=|g|\geq 2^{i}.

Therefore |g|=|f|=2i|g|=|f|=2^{i}. Applying the induction assumption for gg, we obtain that gg takes values from the set {−a′,0,a′}\{-a^{\prime},0,a^{\prime}\}, where a′a^{\prime} is a positive real number. Since |f|=|g||f|=|g|, we have h⁡(x)∈{−g⁡(x),g⁡(x)}h(x)\in\{-g(x),g(x)\} for every vertex xx of H⁡(n−1)H(n-1). Thus, ff takes values from the set {−2​a′,0,2​a′}\{-2a^{\prime},0,2a^{\prime}\}. ∎

The main result of this paper is the following.

6 Spectrum of optimal functions

In this section, we discuss the spectrum of functions that are optimal in the space U[i,j]​(n)U_{[i,j]}(n). Theorem 2 and Lemma 16 imply that the spectrum of such functions forms an arithmetic progression with common difference 11 or 22. More precisely, we have the following result.

Corollary 2.

The following statements hold:

  1. 1.

    Let f∈U[i,j]​(n)f\in U_{[i,j]}(n), where i+j≥ni+j\geq n. If |f|=2i|f|=2^{i}, then

    Spec⁡(f)={i,i+d,…,i+k​d},\mathrm{Spec}(f)=\{i,i+d,\ldots,i+kd\},

    where d∈{1,2}d\in\{1,2\}, kk is non-negative integer and i+k​d≤ji+kd\leq j.

  2. 2.

    Let f∈U[i,j]​(n)f\in U_{[i,j]}(n), where i+j≤ni+j\leq n. If |f|=2n−j|f|=2^{n-j}, then

    Spec⁡(f)={j−k​d,j−(k−1)​d,…,j},\mathrm{Spec}(f)=\{j-kd,j-(k-1)d,\ldots,j\},

    where d∈{1,2}d\in\{1,2\}, kk is non-negative integer and j−k​d≥ij-kd\geq i.

Corollary 2 implies that if f∈U[i,j]​(n)f\in U_{[i,j]}(n) and Spec⁡(f)\mathrm{Spec}(f) is not an arithmetic progression of a special kind, then |f|>max⁡(2i,2n−j)|f|>\max(2^{i},2^{n-j}). For example, if f∈U⁡(n)f\in U(n) and Spec⁡(f)={0,3}\mathrm{Spec}(f)=\{0,3\}, where n≥3n\geq 3, then |f|>2n−3|f|>2^{n-3}. In view of these observations, it seems natural to consider the following question.

Problem 5.

Let n≥3n\geq 3. Find

minf∈U⁡(n),Spec⁡(f)={0,3}⁡|f|.\min_{f\in U(n),\mathrm{Spec}(f)=\{0,3\}}|f|.
